full_judgment:
3. The relevant facts for disposal of the Rule, inter alia, are that the petitioner as pre-emptor filed the pre-emption case No. 2 of 2003 against the kabala-purchaser and the other opposite-parties excluding the opposite party No. 7 in the pre-emption case for an order of pre-emption in respect of the property which were sold as stated in the schedule of the pre-emption petition. 

 6. In the said proceeding one Md Kamrul Islam Swpan filed an application under Order No. 1 Rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure for addition of party as the opposite party No. 7 and after hearing the parties the learned court below allowed the application made him as opposite party No. 7. The opposite party No. 7 filed a written objection denying all the material allegations made in the pre-emption petition stating that he has purchased the case land from the opposite party No.1 on 6-1-2003 before receiving the notice for pre-emption and he is in possession of the case land. The added opposite party No. 7 further stated that the pre-emptor is not a contiguous land holder and he has no right for filing the pre-emption case and thus according to him the pre-emption case is liable to be dismissed. 

 7. After hearing the parties and considering the supported documents and witnesses statements made by the parties the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Ulipur, Kurigram dismissed the pre-emption case by its judgment and order dated 22-2-2007. Being aggrieved the present-petitioner as an appellant filed the Miscellaneous Appeal No. 53 of 2007 before the learned District Judge which was heard by the learned Additional District Judge, Ulipur, District-Kurigram on transfer who also dismissed the appeal by affirming the judgment of the trial court. Hence this revisional application and the Rule was obtained thereof. 

 12. Mr Md Shahidul Islam, the learned Advocate appearing with Mr Asaduzzaman Ansari, the learned Advocate, contended that he has purchased the case land from the opposite party No. 1 of the pre-emption case on 6-1-2003 before receiving the notice for pre-emption. He is in possession of the case land not the opposite party No. 1 in the pre-emption case. The learned Advocate further contended that the suit land does not situate contiguous to the land of the pre-emptor and therefore the present pre-emptor has no right to file the pre-emption thus the learned trial court categorically found that there was no cause of action for filing a case for pre-emption and the learned appellate court below concurrently found that this pre-emption case does not come within the ambit of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act for claiming pre-emption thus, the learned appellate court below also dismissed the appeal and thereby committed no error of law. 

 13. The learned Advocate for the opposite party No.1 further submits that the opposite party Nos.1 and 2 are husband and wife and pre-emption has been claimed against the husband of the co-sharer owner which is not tenable under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, as such, the learned appellate court below came to a concurrent lawful decision that a pre-emption cannot be allowed to Continue. The learned Advocate also submits that the trial court by its judgment and order considered the claim made by the pre-emptor in the pre-emption case and considered the submissions made by the PW1, the present pre-emptor petitioner who in his cross-examination clearly deposed that he would not aware as to the land for which he filed the suit and PW 2 was also refused about the land claimed by the pre-emptor hence the trial court lawfully came to a conclusion to dismiss the pre-emption case and the learned appellate court decided on a finding that the pre-emptor and petitioner has also failed to prove its own under the provision of law and found a concurrent decision, hence, the Rule is liable to be discharged and no interference from this court is called for. 

 15. It further appears to me that the present petitioner brought the pre-emption case and filed certain documents which have been exhibited as to his claim. It is an unique case where the opposite party Nos. 1, 2 or other opposite parties in the pre-emption case did not contest the suit but added as opposite party No. 7 came forward by himself and applied to be added in the suit to contest the pre-emption case as being a purchaser of the suit land and it also appears that this added opposite party No. 7 only contested the suit by adducing as many as 8 to 9 exhibits in favour of his ownership even though there was no claim made by the pre-emptor against him. After considering the lower court record and the deposition made by the PWs and DWs it makes clear that why a party was needed to be added as opposite party No. 7. The PW 1 Md Mohiuddin Sheikh deposed in the court that that he claimed land in the Dag Nos. 464 and 74/1273. In the cross-examination he clearly stated that he was not aware for the land he filed the pre-emption case. In this regard the trial court came to a conclusion that the pre-emptor failed to prove its own case on the basis of this finding as follows:— 

 16. It also appears to me that the learned appellate court below considered the documents available in the court along with the judgment of the trial court and concurrently found that the present pre-emptor failed to prove its own case under the provision of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. He accordingly found as follows:— 

 17. After examining both the judgments concurrently finding that the present pre-emptor-petitioner failed to prove that this pre-emption case can come under the provision of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act because the petitioner is not sure which land he was claiming to pre-empt. Even though in his deposition he tried to give a description of his own land thus both the courts concurrently found against the pre-emptor-petitioner. 

 18. Regarding the submission made by the learned Advocate for the pre-emptor as to the provision under section 5 of the Transfer of Property Act contending a doctrine of lis-pendence, I consider that if a case is not filed as per the requirement of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and subsequently the suit is dismissed on that basis by the trial court and also by the appellate court even though the pendency of a case should not be a bar to transfer a land by and between the parties.
